responses:
## Analysis

The last three attempts all changed the code structurally (hoisting the `return` into `n`, peeling the `l == 16` case) but left the cost at exactly 3549. Those rewrites compile to the same SSA, so they don't move the score. The reference cost is 7570, so the current program is already about 2.1x cheaper. The remaining cost is mostly the 16 bounds checks per block, and each `xs[i]` with a constant index carries its own check unless the compiler can prove it safe.

The change below re-slices once with `b := xs[:16]` and indexes the fixed-length `b`. Length 16 is known after the slice, so the per-index checks in the hot 16-word path should be reduced or removed. It does not change the result: `xs[:16]` is valid because `l >= 16` is checked first, and `xs` is only read, never written.

I can't run giri here, so this is unverified. If the interpreter does not eliminate the checks, the cost may stay flat, but it should not be worse by more than the one extra slice instruction per block.
